items.title: I want my Wednesday back
items.summary: php, security
items.content:
Or, why we’re not seeing mass-exploitation of php2shell yet.

I saw wildly varying opinions on whether php2shell is serious, or if they cried wolf. Got curious, started digging into the PoCs. I’m not an exploit dev and maybe there were other factors, so take with a grain of salt. Egg on my face if mass exploitation starts right as I hit publish.

Best PoC of php2shell I’ve found: https://github.com/9bie/php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp (and a fork with all docs translated to english )

To exploit, you need to do four consecutive requests to the same php worker process . And you need to know the exact php build (php version, OS version, architecture), or try exploits for every possible build.

What this PoC does is take a docker image that uses the default mod_php number of workers, which is 150. Then it opens 149 connections that send half a request to keep the other workers busy, and does the four exploit requests against the 150th worker.

Even a moderately popular production website will have multiple web VMs/containers running multiple php workers behind a load balancer and constant bot traffic. That means you would have to try a wide range of number of connections to open. On top of that you likely won’t know the exact build version, so you would have to try exploits for every combination out there.

Let’s say you try this for the 50 most popular php/OS combinations, and any number of workers between 10 and 1010. That’s 50k attempts. But against constant background traffic, you would need to try each combination a number of times. Each of these attempts involves opening a whole lot of connections, so they each take some time. The PoC runs against localhost and takes 3-4 seconds, so let’s optimistically call it 10 seconds on the internet.

You can only do one attempt at a time, so that means multiple days of bruteforcing in a way that is essentially a DoS, since a large part of that range will exhaust the maximum number of connections. At this point the person running the site will likely notice, start blocking IP addresses or adding a WAF.

Most high-traffic websites already run WAFs/rate-limiting to deal with bot traffic, so you would need to run this attack from a great many IPs, and preferably clean ones that are harder to come by. But running this from many IPs also increases the chances that your timing will be off, reducing the number of plausible attempts even further.

That’s assuming the WAF doesn’t block your attempts entirely, because the easiest ways to exploit these vulnerabilities were known at the time of the announcement.

I’m sure people and agents will come up with clever techniques to reduce the required number of attempts eventually. But that has nothing to do with “this will get mass-exploited within 15 minutes.”

Against very low-traffic websites that do not have any bot protection, leak information about their version, running close to stock configuration, you might get lucky.

So sure, it’s a critical vulnerability, deserves attention, should be patched ASAP. Maybe even put in the announcement that if you’re running low-traffic sites, be extra sure to patch fast.

But to the AI security vendors who promoted this as THE GATES OF HELL WILL OPEN YOU HAVE TO PATCH WITHIN 15 MINUTES OR DIE? I want my Wednesday back.

Oh and the claims of it being exploited in the wild? At time of writing, they’re referring to exploitation attempts . In fact, HoneyLabs so far hasn’t seen a single exploit attempt that could even run successfully.

items.content_ko: 작성자는 php2shell이 아직 대량 악용되지 않는 이유를 살펴보려고 PoC를 분석했다고 밝히며, 자신은 익스플로잇 개발자가 아니므로 다른 요인이 있을 수 있다고 전제합니다. 작성자가 찾은 가장 나은 PoC(9bie/php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp, 문서를 영문으로 번역한 포크 포함)는 같은 PHP 워커 프로세스에 요청 네 개를 연속으로 보내야 하며, 정확한 PHP 빌드(PHP 버전, OS 버전, 아키텍처)를 알거나 가능한 모든 빌드에 대해 시도해야 합니다. 이 PoC는 기본 mod_php 워커 수인 150개를 쓰는 Docker 이미지를 대상으로, 149개의 연결을 열어 절반만 보낸 요청으로 다른 워커들을 붙잡아 두고 150번째 워커에 익스플로잇 요청 네 개를 보냅니다. 작성자는 실제 운영 웹사이트는 로드 밸런서 뒤에 여러 웹 VM과 컨테이너, 여러 PHP 워커가 있고 지속적인 봇 트래픽이 있어서, 열어야 할 연결 수를 넓은 범위로 바꿔 가며 시도해야 한다고 설명합니다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
items.content:
We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.

We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.

Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai , Kimi Work , Kimi Code , and the Kimi API . The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.

Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%) . And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon , our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2% , above K3's 55.95% .

K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.

K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot , combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:

K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.

K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools , approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.

K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry,…

items.summary_ko: C/C++에서 정의되지 않은 동작(UB)이 실제로 어떤 결과를 낳는지 어셈블리 예시로 보여주는 글이다. 일부 사람들은 UB가 문제없다고 주장하지만, 널 포인터 역참조 같은 코드는 컴파일러가 예상치 못한 기계어를 생성할 수 있다. 본문은 `std::unreachable()`을 `int* ptr = nullptr; *ptr = 99;`로 바꾸면 생성되는 코드에서 99가 아닌 0이 주소 0에 기록된 뒤 잘못된 명령으로 프로그램이 종료되는 과정을 보여준다.
items.content_ko: 본문은 메모리 매핑 장치를 제어하는 가상의 코드를 예로 든다. `std::unreachable()`은 해당 지점에서 정의되지 않은 동작을 일으킨다고 정의되어 있다. 이 경우 컴파일러는 `device_command`에 42를 쓰는 어셈블리를 생성하고, 이후 명령은 실행된다고 설명한다. 널 포인터 역참조 예시도 다룬다. 사람들은 주소 0에 접근하면 보통 세그먼트 폴트가 난다고 생각하지만, 컴파일된 결과는 다르다. 주소 0에 0이 먼저 기록되고, 이후 잘못된 명령으로 프로그램이 중단된다. 99는 생성된 프로그램에 나타나지 않지만, 널 포인터 쓰기는 실제로 남는다. 저자는 이것이 디버거의 오류 메시지를 개선하기 위한 것일 수 있다고 추측한다. 마지막에는 생성된 어셈블리 예시가 몇 개 더 제시된다.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

마치 테러리스트가 인질극 벌이는데 인질 죽는다고 테러리스트 진압 안하겠다는 것과 같은 말이다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

items.title: The glorious @xkcdRandom Zig builtin
items.summary: compilers, satire, zig
items.content:
One of my favorite xkcd comics of all time is Random Number . The image depicts a C function that supposedly returns a random integer, but in reality always returns 4 . I was reminded of this wonderful comic a few days ago, due to a security incident where people accidentally used the number 4 (among others) instead of a properly generated sequence of random bytes. Satire has a tendency to become reality, I guess.

Since there is a clear demand among developers for the xkcd random number generator, I’m of the opinion that self-respecting languages should ship a built-in implementation. I’m here today to lead by example, as I unveil the glorious @xkcdRandom builtin for the Zig language. Can you guess what it does? Indeed, it returns the number 4 ! Now go found a multi-billion-dollar startup on top of this genius idea.

Why not? After completing the Ziglings exercises and brain-coding a toy minesweeper game , I felt like my grasp of the language was solid enough to attempt something more ambitious. I wanted to get my hands on production-grade Zig code, and play with it to see how the different pieces of the language fit together. Hacking on the Zig compiler sounded like the perfect idea!

A sane person might implement the xkcd RNG as a literal port of the original C code, which maps to the following Zig function:

There’s one very big drawback to this approach: it’s boring. Don’t get me wrong, I like boring and low-maintenance code as much as the next person… but this time my goal is to learn , not to produce . I actually want to jump through hoops and make things overly complicated! Builtins are perfect for this. They are, as the name suggests, built-in constructs in the Zig language. Adding one means I get to fork and modify the compiler. Yay!

The builtin source code is intertwined with the rest of the Zig compiler, so it’s not really possible to include it here. Feel free to inspect the diff if you are curious (it’s just 22 lines), or to clone my Zig fork and check out the 0.17.x-xkcd branch.

With these changes to the compiler, you can build programs like the one below. Isn’t that neat?

The Zig developers have clearly put effort into developer experience. You can build Zig with a single command: zig build --zig-lib=lib -Dno-lib -Ddev=x86_64-linux . The fresh build took roughly a minute to complete on my laptop, which in my book is quite good for a compiler. Subsequent builds were faster.

As for the coding work itself, an LLM pointed me to the file where builtins were defined, and I took over from there: modifying things, checking for compile errors, fixing them, and so on. The code was easy to navigate, thanks to its clear structure and the Zig language server’s help. I was done way faster than I expected! Maybe I should find a real compiler issue to tackle next.

Did it work? Yes, it did! Once I had everything in place, I built the modified Zig, compiled the example program from above, ran it, and watched it output the 100% guaranteed random numbers:

items.title: How Block Blast harvests its players for ad money
items.content:
I posted a video about this game that got over 15 million views, so I wanted to do the full technical write-up: the code, and how you can reproduce it yourself.

Some context on why it matters: between January and May 2026, Block Blast made an estimated $127 million from ads. Candy Crush Saga made $81.1 million over the same months (Sensor Tower estimates).

Most of Block Blast isn’t in the app you install

We started with the Android app, version 10.8.2. We decompiled the Java side with jadx and the native Cocos library with Ghidra, and found almost nothing interesting in the package you download from the store. Block Blast is built from small modules the code calls traits, and each trait has variants called arms. Running it on a clean Android 14 emulator with no account and watching its cache and logcat showed how it works: when the app launches, the server sends a config that says which arm of which trait you get, and the app downloads them as encrypted JavaScript. The config my install got names about 700 traits. My install selected 254 of them, and 101 were downloaded after install.

items.title_ko: Block Blast가 광고 수익을 위해 플레이어를 활용하는 방식
items.summary_ko: 작성자가 1,500만 회 이상 조회된 영상의 후속으로 공개한 기술 분석입니다. 작성자는 2026년 1~5월 Block Blast의 광고 수익을 추정치 1억 2,700만 달러로 제시하며, 같은 기간 Candy Crush Saga의 8,110만 달러(Sensor Tower 추정)와 비교합니다. 안드로이드 앱 10.8.2를 분석한 결과, 스토어에서 받는 패키지에는 흥미로운 내용이 거의 없고 서버 설정에 따라 암호화된 JavaScript를 내려받는 구조라고 설명합니다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 안드로이드 앱 10.8.2를 jadx(Java)와 Ghidra(네이티브 Cocos 라이브러리)로 분석했지만, 스토어에서 받는 패키지에서는 거의 찾지 못했다고 밝힙니다. Block Blast는 'trait'이라 부르는 작은 모듈로 구성되고, 각 trait에는 'arm'이라 부르는 변형이 있습니다. 앱을 실행하면 서버가 어떤 trait의 어떤 arm을 쓸지 정하는 설정을 보내고, 앱은 이를 암호화된 JavaScript로 내려받습니다. 계정 없이 깨끗한 Android 14 에뮬레이터에서 캐시와 logcat을 관찰한 결과, 설정에는 약 700개의 trait이 있었고 그중 254개가 선택되었으며 101개는 설치 후에 내려받아졌습니다. 본문은 CTAgloReviveTrait, CTReviveTimeOutSkipSplashTrait, ClassNewDeathOptimizeTrait, DeadlyToHardTrait 같은 trait 이름을 나열하다가 끊깁니다.

items.title: This Week in Plasma: Fixing All the Bugs, PiP, and Performance
items.content:
This Week in Plasma: Fixing All the Bugs, PiP, and Performance

Nate Graham , John Veness , and Farid Abdelnour

Welcome to a new issue of This Week in Plasma. And it’s going to be a big one, folks!

This week, a familiar pattern played out: people upgraded to Plasma 6.8 and found all the bugs that nobody reported during the beta period, and the Plasma team worked incredibly hard to fix them! You’ll see the result below: tons of bug fixes.

It’s clear that not enough people are testing Plasma’s beta releases to uncover and report all regressions. We’re open for ideas on how to improve this.

In addition to the bug fixes, this week also saw a number of nice new features, UI improvements, and performance enhancements. Consequential stuff! Check it out below:

After extended testing, KWin’s support for the Wayland picture-in-picture (PiP) protocol has been deemed stable enough, and turned on by default! (Vlad Zahorodnii, kwin MR #10175 )

Window sizes and positions are now remembered on a per-screen-arrangement basis!

This means if you arrange your open windows across two screens, then disconnect one, then rearrange the windows to suit the now-single-screen arrangement… then when you reconnect the second screen, open windows will jump to the sizes and positions they last had on the two-screen arrangement. And when you disconnect a screen again, open windows will jump to the sizes and positions they had on the single-screen setup.

Note that this only takes effect within a running session for open windows; it does not affect the positioning of windows that are closed and then reopened. That’s still being worked on. (Jakob Petsovits, kwin MR #10198 )

You can now permanently deny XWayland-using apps from asking to control the pointer and keyboard, and also see which apps have been denied and revoke their denials. (David Redondo, KDE Bugzilla #521576 )

In-progress downloads in Firefox that produce a nice native Plasma notification via Plasma Browser Integration can now be paused and resumed from that notification. (Simon Hürlimann, plasma-browser-integration MR #207 )

Plasma Browser Integration now supports the Brave browser. (Geevarghese ST, plasma-browser-integration MR #179 )

The Activity Switcher sidebar no longer stretches wallpaper images for screens without a 16:9 aspect ratio; now the wallpaper is shown faithfully, but cropped if needed. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #478784 )

When you use a plain color as your wallpaper in conjunction with the “accent color from wallpaper” feature, the accent color is now set to the exact color of your wallpaper, not a generated shade of it. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #513851 )

Holding down a key that plays or pauses media now plays or pauses it once, rather than repeatedly. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #521448 )

When using the zoom feature with “Push” pointer tracking, zooming in or out some more will now center the zoom on the pointer’s current location. (Maxim Stomphorst, KDE Bugzilla #508098 )

If you hold down the Shift or Ctrl keys to select multiple items on System Monitor’s Applications or Processes pages, the items in the list views temporarily stop rearranging themselves so you can actually select items properly! (Vladimir Pahomchik, plasma-systemmonitor MR #479 )

System Settings’ Wi-Fi & Networking page now uses the more familiar “forget” terminology for removing networks. (Taras Oleksyn, KDE Bugzilla #525844 )

On System Settings’ Task Switcher page, the feature to preview a new Alt + Tab window switcher style now simply triggers it to appear rather than using a simulation, which ensures that it always looks right. This also fixes a bug that made certain visualizations un-preview-able. (Kai Uwe Broulik, kwin MR #10154 and KDE Bugzilla #508088 )

items.summary_ko: Plasma 6.8 업그레이드 후 베타 기간에 보고되지 않았던 버그들이 많이 드러나, 이번 주에는 대량의 버그 수정이 이뤄졌다고 합니다. KWin의 Wayland 픽처 인 픽처(PiP) 프로토콜 지원은 충분히 안정적이라고 판단되어 기본값으로 켜졌고, 창 크기와 위치는 화면 배치별로 기억되도록 바뀌었습니다.
items.content_ko: Nate Graham, John Veness, Farid Abdelnour가 작성한 이번 주 Plasma 소식입니다. Plasma 6.8 사용자들이 베타 때 보고되지 않았던 버그를 많이 발견했고, 팀이 이를 수정했다고 전합니다. 베타 테스트 참여가 부족해 회귀 버그를 충분히 찾지 못했다며 개선 아이디어를 구하고 있다고 밝힙니다. 주요 변경으로 KWin의 Wayland PiP 프로토콜 지원이 기본 활성화되었고(kwin MR #10175), 창 크기와 위치가 화면 배치 단위로 기억됩니다. 두 화면에 창을 배치했다가 한 화면을 분리한 경우를 예로 드는 대목에서 본문이 끊깁니다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.title: Software is slow because of bad design, not slow languages
items.summary: performance
items.content:
Many people are saying that AI will make software faster by rewriting it in faster languages, but this isn’t generally true. Most programs cannot be meaningfully sped up by rewriting them in C or Rust.

How can this be true? Some languages are orders-of-magnitude faster than others: for instance, C can be fifty times faster than Python. Won’t rewriting my Python program in C thus make it fifty times faster? No, it won’t. Software performance is usually dominated by I/O, not the speed of the language. Where language speed matters, most slow languages already have popular libraries that allow them to unlock C-like speed. In general, performance is a matter of design , not of language choice.

Consider a simple CRUD website with a database. For any given request, 50% of the request time 1 might be spent querying the database: to fetch the current user, the record being asked for, any relevant user memberships or settings, and so on. Rewriting that website in C can only speed up that other 50%, which puts a hard ceiling on the improvements you can make 2 . At best, you’ll make requests twice as fast (probably closer to 1.5x in practice). That’s not bad, but it’s nowhere near an order-of-magnitude speedup.

In other words, most real programs are “I/O-bound”: they spend most of their time waiting for data to be input or output somewhere, as opposed to “CPU-bound” programs that spend most of their time actively doing things. I/O-bound programs don’t just have to rely on a database. Often programs have to wait on some third-party API, or on writing or reading data to disk. You could speed the code in curl up by 100x and you probably wouldn’t even notice, because curl spends all of its time waiting on the network.

Slow languages already delegate work to fast languages

What about work that is obviously not I/O-bound? For instance, wikis have to turn stored markdown into renderable HTML 3 . Wouldn’t rewriting that in a faster language cause a massive speedup? It would! That’s why applications that do that use libraries like cmark-gfm that call out to fast languages for markdown rendering. In general, most slow languages can write very fast programs by invoking this kind of library. Python is famously a slow language, but it’s a competitive choice for CPU-bound workloads like machine learning and mathematics, because it has a healthy set of libraries that let it offload these workloads to fast C code. If a Python program spends 80% of its time doing matrix multiplications on a GPU, you are very unlikely to be able to speed it up by rewriting it in C, because those matrix multiplications are already happening in tightly-optimized C or assembly code.

Of course, some programs do in fact do a lot of CPU-bound work in slow languages. If a program has not had much engineering attention, there will probably be a lot of low-hanging fruit . But these programs are often unimportant: if they were important, someone would have gone in and optimized them already, before AI made it (relatively) easy. That doesn’t mean it’s impossible to find a useful program to rewrite. Actual Computer recently rewrote tiktoken in assembly, providing a significant 4 speedup. However, you’re not going to revolutionize some field of computing like this. Even fast tokenization is only useful on the margins, because time spent in tokenization is a fraction of the time spent in inference.

Speeding up software typically involves a redesign

Despite all this, I think most software is far slower than it could be. I’m optimistic about the potential (with or without AI) to significantly speed up commonly-used software. But I think most of these speedups will come from redesigning the program, not rewriting it in a faster language.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Spotify ramps up policy enforcement on family plans
items.content:
As reported by Music Business Worldwide , Spotify appears to be stepping up enforcement of existing policies regarding Family and Duo subscription plans by requiring users to scan a QR code in person on the plan manager’s device in order to maintain access to it. Those who fail to scan the address verification QR code within seven days will see their account demoted to the free tier and be barred from joining any other Duo or Family plan for 12 months.

Spotify’s support documentation verifies the policy after users on Reddit began posting reports of receiving the QR prompt. The enforcement stems from Spotify’s requirement that family plan members reside at the same address—a seemingly reasonable policy in concept. But what if you have a child away in college, a spouse who works on the road, or any number of other circumstances that might see families separated by physical distance? The policy could extend beyond friend groups looking to save a buck, affecting actual families who thought they were using the program as intended.

Goldman Sachs analysts, in their October 15 Music in the Air: 10 Years On  report, made available by HITS Daily Double , estimate that “a meaningful share of family plan users are not actual household members, but rather friends sharing a plan to reduce costs.” The report goes on to add, “We see additional monetization upside from tightening household verification on multi-user plans. Most family plans require members to reside at the same address, but enforcement has been minimal in practice.”

If the pressure on the accounts policy from Wall Street sounds familiar, it should. Streaming services have often turned a blind eye to account sharing during their growth periods, only to walk back the leniency once viewers are hooked. Netflix tweeted in March of 2017 that “ Love is sharing a password ” before launching its own enforcement policies in May of 2023 . Later that year, Netflix raised prices up to 17 percent , and by April of 2024, the company saw the policy pay off with 9.3 million added subscriptions and a 54 percent bump in operating income. Netflix isn’t alone in the practice, as competitors like Max (now HBO again) and Disney+/Hulu eventually followed suit with their own policy enforcement.

Goldman’s report argues that while family plans are great for getting subscribers onto the platform, “the per-user monetization of these plans materially lags individual plan pricing. In our view, these plans offer a greater value proposition to consumers than the standard individual tier, which we believe gives DSPs the opportunity to capture more value through higher pricing increases or by tightening the definition/eligibility of the family plan, without meaningfully impacting demand.” In short, analysts are confident that music streaming services such as Spotify can enforce strict account policies, raise prices, and still make more money.

So if you go to load up your favorite playlist on a shared account, you might soon be getting a warning that it’s time to check in with your plan manager. If that’s physically impossible to do within seven days, you might need to look into an alternative streaming service—or start digging through drawers until you find that old iPod.

Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Canadians are running out of time to oppose Bill C-22
items.content:
Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate.

Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.)

As we wrote earlier this year , Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic insecurity.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on.

It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime.

Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime.

Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users without any Canadian court oversight.

Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution.

If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality.

Canadians: defend your privacy and security

items.title: Indian government sites are serving revoked eMudhra certificates
items.summary: security
items.content:
On 17th October, eight eMudhra intermediate CAs chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 were found to have trivially recoverable private keys . They were revoked the next day, and Mozilla and Chrome are now distrusting the G3 root. Separately, on 19th October eMudhra revoked 9,356 certificates on its unaffected RSA hierarchy (emSign Root CA - G1) with the reason “Superseded”. That batch matches every unexpired certificate missing a certificate-type policy OID required by emSign’s own CP/CPS ( Bug 2082782 ).

On 21st October, MeitY posted this thread :

A security incident concerning eMudhra’s Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) was reported in the public domain. […]

However, some social media accounts are indulging in fear mongering about the impact of this incident. […]

The impact of this incident on Indian websites and applications have been very limited and for a very short interval.

— @GoI_MeitY , 21st October 2026, 16:31 CEST

That last claim is wrong on both counts. The interval wasn’t short: the flawed keys were generated in April 2025, so anyone could have recovered them for 18 months before the report. The impact isn’t limited either: the compromised intermediates barely issued anything, but Mozilla and Chrome are now distrusting the entire G3 root, so eMudhra estimates 30,000 certificates from its unaffected G3 intermediates must be migrated. From what I could see, most of those seem to belong to US universities using eMudhra through InCommon rather than Indian sites.

Meanwhile, the 19th October revocations have left Indian government sites serving revoked certificates days later , including four bodies under MeitY itself: STPI , Bhashini , UIDAI , and the Controller of Certifying Authorities, whose India PKI site is serving a revoked eMudhra certificate. Notably, Controller of Certifying Authorities regulates eMudhra’s CA business in India.

I checked the 8,947 hosts in the IGOD directory of Indian government websites. As of 23rd October, 156 of them are still serving one of these revoked certificates. All of them were revoked between 15:34 and 15:49 CEST on 19th October, and are listed in eMudhra’s CRLs for DV/G2A-1 , OV/G2A-1 , EV/G2A-1 and G1 .

Whether these sites open depends on your browser. Firefox ships CRLite , which covers every revocation, and refuses to load them. Chrome’s CRLSet (version 10856, 24th October) has none of these certificates, nor any of the 6,235 entries on the DV/G2A-1 CRL, so Chrome, Edge and Android load them fine. So does Safari on iOS, which only checks OCSP for EV certificates. Two sites on the list have one: www.isea.gov.in and nfscnagpur.nic.in , and emSign’s OCSP responder reports the isea.gov.in certificate as revoked, so Safari on iOS refuses to load it. SSL Labs checks the CRL itself and marks all of these as Grade F / revoked.

Revocations happen (GoDaddy just revoked 4 lakh certificates), but they are usually accompanied by notifications to subscribers to

get them to new valid certificates. I’m not sure if eMudhra is doing any of the sort, now that they don’t care about their TLS business.

The table will be updated with timestamps as cert rotations happen.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Native masonry layouts with CSS grid lanes
items.content:
Save 20% on all of our high quality, premium courses using the code NEXTLEVEL at checkout

Native masonry layouts have been a long time coming to CSS and after years of debate over how they should work and fit into the language, we finally have display: grid-lanes .

If you want the full backstory on how we got here, Sunkanmi Fafowora has a great overview of the grid-lanes announcement over on CSS-Tricks. Here, I want to focus on the technical side of masonry, why it took so long to get right, and how display: grid-lanes works.

Masonry has been a long-running CSS challenge. Back in 2017, Rachel Andrew opened a CSSWG issue about creating a native Pinterest-style layout. As Rachel noted back then, the closest native CSS got to this was multi-column layout (column-count), but that flows items top-to-bottom. Masonry needs to flow items across rows, tightly packing them into whatever column currently has the most available vertical space.

That same year, Tab Atkins-Bittner shared a clever Grid hack to approximate the layout. It relied on knowing each item’s height in advance, making it less practical for dynamic content.

As cool as this hack was, having to know the exact height of every item ahead of time wasn’t very practical, especially when you’re dealing with dynamic content, where heights can change. When I spoke with Tab Atkins-Bittner for my piece on the evolution of CSS Masonry , they put the broader challenge of designing CSS layouts this way:

“Flexbox was the first of the modern layout algorithms; we made a lot of mistakes and missteps while writing it, because we were trying to figure out how a modern layout model should work.”

That same process of figuring things out played a role in masonry’s development and until CSS had a better answer, many of us ended up reaching for David DeSandro’s legendary Masonry.js library instead.

But the challenge wasn’t just figuring out how to make masonry work in CSS. There was also the question of how it should fit into the language. Should it be part of Flexbox, an extension of Grid, or its own display value? For years, the CSS Working Group went back and forth without settling on a final syntax.

Mozilla first explored adding masonry to Grid, and WebKit later picked up that approach. It lets you keep display: grid and use a special value for the tracks to enable masonry.

This kept Grid’s familiar column definitions while letting the browser pack items vertically instead of aligning them into rows. You can read more about WebKit’s reasoning in Help us choose the final syntax for Masonry in CSS .

Google’s Chromium team had a different take. They argued that masonry’s layout algorithm was different enough from Grid to deserve its own layout mode, proposed as display: masonry .

Their reasoning, along with an alternative syntax, is explained in An alternative proposal for CSS masonry .

The debate continued through several rounds of proposals, including WebKit’s broader item-flow idea for unifying aspects of Grid and Flexbox, but that approach was eventually dropped in favor of a simpler direction.

In January 2025, the CSS Working Group agreed to reuse CSS Grid’s track-definition and placement properties for masonry. By December 2025, the group had settled on a name for the new layout mode, grid-lanes . WebKit announced the direction in Introducing CSS Grid Lanes .

The nice thing about display: grid-lanes is that you don’t have to figure out where every item goes yourself. You define the tracks along one axis, just as you would with regular CSS Grid and the browser handles placement along the other.

For a typical masonry layout, that means defining your columns with grid-template-columns and letting the browser stack items into whichever lane makes the most sense.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

items.title: Dessa: Conversation Model trained only on speech
items.content:
We believe voice is the most natural way to interact with intelligence, so we created Dessa, the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built. Talking with it feels like talking with a person…full of emotion, nuance, pauses, and a natural cadence.

Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous.

We trained Dessa from scratch on nothing but human conversation. Sounds! No text, no pretrained models. It learned to hold a real-time conversation simply by listening. As far as we know, Dessa is the world’s first AI you can have a realistic live conversation with that was trained only from human speech.

Dessa advances the frontier of deep learning models and creates a different category with entirely new and interesting behaviors for researchers to discover. How efficiently do they learn language and facts compared to text? How efficiently can they learn new languages? What sorts of In-context learning can they perform?

Every clip below is a live recording of a person talking to Dessa. Nobody steers it. Dessa picks what to say, when to say it and how, down to its own voice and personality. Subtitles were added afterward.

It laughs the moment something’s funny, mid-sentence, the way people do. Other models wait for you to finish, then laugh on cue. Ask it to speak up and it gets louder. Nobody taught it that.

The person blanks on a movie title. Dessa finishes the sentence. It also knows a surprising amount, considering every fact it has come from raw sound.

A surprise. Dessa gasps “oh my god” under its breath, then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude.

In this demo, Dessa is talking with GPT-Live-1, a third-party AI model. Both voices are AI-generated. The developer of GPT-Live-1 is not affiliated with Block and has not reviewed or endorsed Dessa.

More recordings will be shared on X soon.

Audio in, audio out. Dessa is a true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech. It’s full-duplex, so it listens and talks at the same time, like you do. It learned from real conversation, so it knows when to cut in and when to backchannel (“yeah!”, “got it!”, “ooh”) to show it’s with you. Inference runs faster than real time, so there’s no awkward wait. And it runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better.

It natively hears and speaks emotion, sarcasm, laughter, a frustrated sigh, a voice cracking with sadness. Run speech through text and all of that is gone, which is why most voice AI feels stilted, slow and, worst of all, annoying.

LLMs need an insane amount of text. Dessa learned language from hundreds of times fewer words (in fairness, LLMs also have to learn C++ and whatever the hell Angular is).

And it had to learn far more than language. Accents, pauses, breathing, sarcasm, humor, inflection, emotion, when to cut in: every one changes what someone means. Say “I didn’t say she stole my CUDA code” out loud, stressing a different word each time. Same words, different meaning every time.

Speech never repeats. Say a sentence twice, exactly the same way, and the data still comes out different. Text is identical no matter who types it. And a single spoken word takes thousands of times more bytes than the same word in text. People learn to talk so easily that we forget how hard it is. For a machine with no text to lean on, it’s brutal.

But, we figured it out. And we figured out how to train Dessa on only one NVIDIA GB200 NVL72.

Three reasons: curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety.

Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.

items.title: How close can pure FP get to C?
items.summary: performance, programming
items.content:
In Why Lean is Faster Than Rust , the author shares an impressive result: a DEFLATE compression library written in Lean 4 , a functional programming language and proof assistant, outperforming an equivalent Rust package that crates.io says has been downloaded over a billion times. From the article:

lean-zip beats every single compression level miniz_oxide provides, i.e. we're capable of providing the same compression at higher throughput. At its fastest setting we're 15% quicker and the output is 8.8% smaller.

However, the article also notes that while they managed to surpass Rust's miniz_oxide , they were no match for the end boss of DEFLATE performance: libdeflate , written in C.

lean-zip is certainly not the best here: libdeflate unsurprisingly blows it out of the water (unsurprisingly because this is a very carefully tuned implementation using architecture-specific SIMD, that we can't touch in Lean).

Enter Roc , a functional programming language (but not a theorem prover) with an explicit focus on runtime performance.

Roc's tagline is "Fast, Friendly, Functional," and Fast comes first because both running fast and compiling fast have always been central goals. Roc is not a mature language (it's still weeks away from its first numbered release, 0.1.0), and its nascent package ecosystem has had almost no optimization work done on it. Still, between its language design, longstanding optimizations , and brand-new compiler implementation , I figured Roc already had enough of a foundation in place to take on the champ: libdeflate.

So I spent a bunch of time grinding through performance optimizations on roc-deflate , a package Niclas Ahden wrote (and uses in paid production work ) for DEFLATE compression. I didn't expect to beat libdeflate's performance across the board, but I wanted to see how close it could get on the non-streaming APIs (as roc-deflate hasn't implemented streaming yet), using the classic Silesia corpus for benchmarking and verifying that it produced identical outputs.

Here's where the benchmarks stand today, running on the 2021 M1 MacBook Pro where I did all the optimization work, as well as on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X Ubuntu machine for an x64 comparison.

roc-deflate ran these 144 benchmarks slower on average than libdeflate, in the median case 8.9% slower on the Ryzen 3900X, and 2.6% on the M1 MacBook Pro.

So while we didn't outperform the champ on average, a median slowdown percentage in the single digits compared to such a carefully-tuned SIMD-powered C library is wild. It's frankly not a result I knew was achievable going in, since Roc is a functional language with automatic memory management racing against code that doesn't have to do bounds checks. (Bounds checks have a cost, but then again, the last time a skipped bounds check in C compression code led to a major Remote Code Execution vulnerability was yesterday .)

The graph shows more detail than just the median gap. On the worst-case inputs, roc-deflate was 18% slower than libdeflate, but on the best-case inputs, roc-deflate was slightly over 18% faster! That's not because Roc has some magical optimization that C can't access; it's just that the two implementations are different, and although on average roc-deflate is slower, for certain inputs it happens to be faster. So while it's possible to get a speedup by switching from libdeflate to roc-deflate, you shouldn't expect it on average.

To be clear, C's performance ceiling is higher than Roc's. For any input where roc-deflate currently outperforms libdeflate, C code can close that gap. The reverse is not true; Roc code is memory-safe, does automatic reference counting, checks bounds, and supports no Rust-style unsafe to opt out of any of that. These properties give Roc code stronger safety guarantees than code written in C, Zig, Rust, and other languages that allow full access to the hardware—and the price it pays for those guarantees is a lower performance ceiling.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising: Turning on Personal Intelligence gives the company more data for ad targeting.
items.content:
Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.

On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy , spotted by Android Authority . The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.

Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads.

Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads.

This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026 , allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.

Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.

According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:

“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”

Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.

A Google spokesperson tells Ars that its privacy clarification does not indicate a change in how it handles your data with respect to its advertising partners. It’s not scanning your entire inbox to enhance your advertising profile, and it’s not giving any of this data to third parties. But if you pipe personal data into an AI search tool, the ads it shows you could be based on that information.

The core of the problem is that Google wants its products and services to talk to each other. Google sees that wealth of data as a key strength of its AI efforts. Some apps like Gmail are still given protected status in Google’s data handling, but there are now more avenues for that data to get out. The more data you share across Google’s ecosystem, the greater the risk to your privacy.

We’ve seen a similar exception in the way Google uses your AI interactions for model training . While Google says it doesn’t use personal data for AI training, it does use your inputs and the model outputs for that purpose. With Gemini integrated with so many services and connected to them via Personal Intelligence, those outputs may very well contain elements of your personal information. Google has said it tries to filter that content from the user activity controls, therefore keeping it out of training sets. However, it doesn’t promise it will always be successful.

items.title: Court reverses San Jose robbery conviction over warrantless cell phone tracking
items.content:
By Robert Salonga | rsalonga@bayareanewsgroup.com | Bay Area News Group

PUBLISHED: October 23, 2026 at 12:37 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 23, 2026 at 4:06 PM PDT

Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

SAN JOSE — An appellate court has thrown out a man’s 2025 robbery conviction after ruling that San Jose police investigators improperly obtained his cell phone records without a warrant, rejecting the police claim of an emergency despite the absence of an active crime and the fact they were already watching him.

In a written opinion Tuesday that reversed the trial court’s conviction of Marcos Andres Andrade — who pleaded no contest to second-degree robbery — the 6th District Court of Appeal determined police violated his Fourth Amendment rights when they cited exigent circumstances to request his real-time cell phone tracking data from Verizon.

Justices pointedly criticized police for bypassing warrant requirements, especially in light of their active surveillance of Andrade in connection with the March 2022 armed carjacking and robbery, and a detective’s later admission that judges usually expedited their warrant requests.

“Our review of the record has persuaded us that the evidence here does not support a determination that investigators in this case reasonably believed they were confronted with an ’emergency situation requiring swift action to prevent imminent danger to life or serious damage to property, or to forestall the imminent escape of a suspect or destruction of evidence,'” Presiding Justice Mary Greenwood wrote in the ruling, quoting prior case law.

Greenwood, leading a three-judge panel, added that their ruling should govern similar investigations going forward.

“Under these circumstances, it appears that investigators in this case submitted the emergency request to Verizon for general investigative purposes, in contravention of the Fourth Amendment. … Thus, applying the exclusionary rule in this case would act to deter similar searches that are devoid of articulable facts to support a request for a defendant’s location data,” Greenwood said.

The ruling also reverses Santa Clara County Superior Court Judge Erik Johnson’s December 2024 order denying Andrade’s motion to suppress the cell phone data. The case now goes back to trial court, with the cell phone data disallowed.

Andrade, who already completed a four-year prison sentence through a combination of jail and prison time, is now permitted to withdraw his no-contest plea that was negotiated with prosecutors. Additionally, the appellate court ordered Johnson and attorneys to re-assess “whether evidence other than the location data of Andrade’s cell phone should be suppressed as the fruits of the illegally obtained location data.”

“We welcome the Court of Appeal’s ruling which confirms that officers cannot simply claim, without evidence, that an emergency exists in order to obtain the cell site location data of community members without a judicial warrant supported by probable cause,” Deputy Public Defender Steven Otero, who represented Andrade, told this news organization. “The court’s ruling ensures the continued protection of our right to be free from warrantless government intrusions into the vast and deeply personal data stored on our cell phones in the absence of a true emergency.”

The district attorney’s office said in a statement, “We are reviewing the decision and deciding our next steps.” The police department said in statement that it “is aware of the court’s ruling and is reviewing its decision,” and deferred further comment to the City Attorney’s Office, which did not respond to an inquiry Friday.

Andrade and Jesus Ivan Larios were both suspected of brandishing guns to rob two people and take their car in the early morning hours of March 1, 2022. San Jose police detectives tracked signals from victims’ phones, which were among the items taken, to an apartment complex on Fontaine Street, where they found the stolen car abandoned.

items.title: Docker is weird
items.summary: programming
items.content:
I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird . Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker.

Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc.

There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat.

Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network.

Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root ) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash , Docker is going to:

Docker’s container runtime, runc , is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Go’s runtime is natively multi-threaded. That’s a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc .

Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Go’s runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls.

Go also doesn’t have fork! Fork only forks the main thread, so it’s kind of a footgun in a runtime like Go’s. But a container runtime really wants to fork, set up a bunch of restrictions, and then exec the process you actually put in docker run . To get around this, runc execs /proc/self/exe with a special command line arguement that identifies it as a child process to approximate a fork.

This is pretty easy to miss if you, like me, run Docker in MacOS. Many of the Linux kernel APIs that container runtimes use require, or at least used to, to be run as root, so the Docker daemon usually runs as root. I can only imagine that container security is a very tough job.

This seems better these days. The big exception seems to be networking. If you’re running a rootless container runtime, it looks like it has to reimplement the whole networking stack in userspace to actually give you the same features!

I’ve only just started my own container runtime, and I already feel like I’ve learned so much about Docker. Writing your own version of a tool you use is a great way to learn about it!

items.title: Sunsetting decomp.dev
items.content:
decomp.dev was born in 2024 as a way to centralize matching decompilation progress and to help expand a community of talented, like-minded folks.

Historically, matching decompilation has been a brutally difficult, time consuming task, on the scale of years for any moderately-sized game with a number of active contributors. As we developed better tooling and shared knowledge around the intricacies of decompilation, the compilers, and the games themselves, progress began to accelerate.

AI's use in decompilation has been experimented with for years, with mixed results. Starting with the release of Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 in early 2026, it was clear that the models were being trained on matching decompilation (they appeared to know our specific tools and how to use them without explicit guidance), and could achieve decent results inside of an established, clean codebase with exhaustive documentation. However, those results still required a significant amount of human cleanup and fixes for obvious issues or cheating (code that technically compiles to the same machine code, but could not be reasonably passed as what the original developers wrote), and the cost per task was prohibitively expensive relative to the results.

Recent models (like GPT-6-Astra) shifted things even further: they are significantly better at following complex directions, cross-referencing resources for symbols or debug information, and writing natural code with enough guidance. They are also exceptionally good permuters: they can write small scripts that test many different source code forms and combinations to find a match, even across files and headers to cover aspects like inlined helpers, signature changes, and operation ordering. In addition, their ability to remain coherent and focused across long-horizon tasks allows them to work continuously without going off the rails. Finally, they can achieve these better results faster and cheaper than earlier models could.

It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way. What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken. Our projects have always been open source to encourage contributions and to benefit the community as a whole. Bad actors have been abusing this in increasingly troublesome ways:

decomp.dev was originally designed to gamify decompilation: watching the progress go up was a fun way to stay motivated when every fraction of a percent took real human effort. Today, that same idea has warped decompilation into a hollow numbers game, exacerbated by folks who just want to burn tokens to make number go up or "port game to PC", all else be damned. While the increased attention has brought in genuine folks who want to learn and contribute meaningfully, I believe that decomp.dev serving as a public index and leaderboard is now causing more harm than good.

decomp.dev will continue to track existing projects and serve individual project pages and historical data, but the main index and adding new projects are disabled.

No. decomp.dev's repository has never had an open source license, and I continue to reserve all rights to the (entirely human written) code. Any replica must not use decomp.dev's code in any form.

I have long held the opinion that AI is not the issue by itself, and we now know it can help tremendously when used correctly. "Slop" comes in many forms, is hard to define, and even harder to moderate. As a sole hobbyist, I don't have the energy (or desire) to define what makes a "good" decompilation and enforce that consistently across the hundreds of projects on the site.

As this era of decompilation comes to a close, I want to thank everyone who's been involved and contributed to our projects, communities and tools. The people and passion behind these projects have always been what's made them fun and rewarding.

items.title: KDE Plasma 6.9 Stabilizes KWin's Wayland Picture-In-Picture Support
items.content:
KDE Plasma 6.9 Stabilizes KWin's Wayland Picture-In-Picture Support

Written by Michael Larabel in KDE on 23 October 2026 at 08:56 PM EDT. 6 Comments

With the wonderful KDE Plasma 6.8 having shipped just more than one week ago, KDE developers are beginning to go heavy on new features for Plasma 6.9.

Most excitingly for the week, the KWin's compositor support for Wayland's Picture-In-Picture (PIP) protocol has been declared stable and enabled by default for Plasma 6.9. Web browsers and other users of the Wayland picture-in-picture support can now enjoy a nice out-of-the-box experience with Plasma 6.9:

And in other Plasma developments, the Plasma Browser Integration now supports the Brave web browser.

Meanwhile the upcoming Plasma 6.8.2 point release is seeing fixes for issues with multi-monitor setups and a variety of other regressions.

More details on these latest KDE Plasma developments can be found via This Week in Plasma .
